Yes. I played that DI in the second round to cancel a Restructure. I

Besides this decks gains enough pool to put many War Ghouls in play,
and, to top it all, I was keeping my War Ghouls untapped as long as
possible when I thought they could be stolen before I could launch a
final attack with them.

> It may be just me but I'm not prepared to play an ally deck now unless
> I have considerable defense from theft as allies and imbued are so
> common now, inclusion of many multiples of cards like entrancement etc
> is nearly always worth while...

But they need stealth too to get those actions through. The Unmasking,
Mr Winthrop and my Auspex cards can help me block some of those ally-
stealing actions. And so can help me leaving my War Ghouls untapped
until needed (as long as there are locations in play) :-)

> What did the other dudes in the final play?

My predator was playing a Guruhi deck with some permacept, permableed,
and Animalism combat.

My prey was playing a Dementation & Obfuscate bleed deck (!Malks and
Malks).

My grandprey was playing a Toreador vote deck with some Toreador Grand
Ball, Alastor (Assault Rifle)...

And my grandpredator was playing an imbued deck (he got 3 game wins in
the prelimary rounds and was top seed).

On my first turn I put Jake Washington in play, and had him employ
Tasha Morgan. Then I brought out Bloodfeud. On my next turn, Jake bled
for 1 :)

The imbued set up very quickly, as usual, and the Toreador was not
drawing his Toreador Grand Balls, so he got his political actions
either Determined or blocked.

My predator was bleeding me for 1-3 each turn, but I had enough pool
gain (via a few Blood Dolls) to bring out several War Ghouls with Lady
Zara Slatikov.

I torporized one of my prey's !Malkavians and let Rudolfo ready so
that he could put pressure on the Toreador.

Later in the game I played Sybil's Tongue to get Break the Code and
put it in play in my discard phase, so that my War Ghouls and the
Guruhi could attack the imbued when the time came (i.e., to stop the
imbued from getting his first VP), since I knew that the game was
going to time out, and I could not let anyone get a VP.

I decided to start the ousting process of my prey when there were ca.
30 minutes left. The imbued player was talking all the time (both
during his turn and during other player's turns). He was always asking
permission to take actions like the one granted by Travis' special
ability, Powers, etc. (thus wasting aiming for the time out).

I had Bloodfeud, Lady Zara, Guedado, Vagabond Mystic, 1 Procurer and 4
War Ghouls in play. So I played Carver's Packing and Storage, bled for
1 with each vampire and torporized my prey's two ready vampires (which
forced him to burn 2 pool due to Tension in the Ranks -controlled by
the imbued-). That left my prey down to 1 pool.

I ousted him on my predator's next turn (via a bounced bleed).

Then I told my prey I would not do anything against him, since the
game was about to time out and I already had the tournament win. But
he called a Banishment, which I blocked with Bloodfeud (who had a Mr
Winthrop), since it was going to target Lady Zara. So on my next turn
I played Fame on Alexandra, since I was afraid she was going to call a
PTO, and launched my 4 War Ghouls against her. Alexandra played 2
Majesty and the War Ghouls could only torporize one of the vampires
who got in their way (but not Alexandra). Then I played Dragonbound.

On his next turn, my prey played Toreador Grand Ball and Alexandra
unblockably called a PTO on Lady Zara, which passed.

Then the imbued rushed Guedado with Ossian and left him empty with a
Pulled Fangs, and thereafter he rushed Bloodfeud with an imbued
bearing an Ivory Bow at "+1 stealth", so Guedado waked and played
basic My Enemy's Enemy to block and went into torpor.

On my next turn, Bloodfeud played Sibyl's Tongue to get the Unmasking
(thus allowing me to leave my War Ghouls untapped waiting for the time
out), But the Tongue got DI'ed by the imbued player. So I rushed
Alexandra again with 2 War Ghouls. Madame Guil got in the way and went
to torpor.

I burned 1 for Dragonbound and ended my turn. During my prey's turn
the game timed out.

There's some truth to your POV, but equating anybody who disagrees as
a "sub par player" is pretty much flamebait. And while there may be
some truth to it, I don't think it's entirely correct either. Jyhad
is a multiplayer game where the posture of one player sends ripples
all around the table, creating effects and facts that the other
players have to deal with, e.g. I'm top seed, I play to wall up, wank
off, and time out. My prey is unhooked. My grandprey is thrown into
a defensive posture, etc etc. Ripples all around, that can perhaps
only be dealt with by all the other non-first seed players agreeing to
set aside the normal pred-prey game and cooperate to unseat the top
guy, or something convoluted like that. And now you're in the same
territory as the argument "it's not broken b/c if the table gangs up
on it, it can be put down." And we all know how strong an argument
*that* is.

I'll close with re-iterating: you've got a point. But it's not an
open and shut case, and the sub-par thing was just asking for a fight
(and, lord knows, if there's one thing I can't stand, it's fighting on
the internet).

Well, yeah. Obviously, if the game has gone on for 3 hours and is at a
complete stalemate, the judge needs to be able and willing to say "ok
guys, I'm giving you one more hour and that's it". Or something.

Never had that problem over here, I think some finals games have
stretched to closed to 3 hours, but that was due to intensive playing,
not stalling. I guess that with a "no time limit" game someone could
still try to stall the game enough to make the judge force a time
limit, but... meh. Haven't seen it myself. At the very least, it
discourages the time-stalling tactics that seem to have become the
norm in tournament finals in some parts of the world -- which is very
good, imho.

...and of course, if someone appears to be stalling, it's a lot easier
for the judge to call him/her on it, since stalling is not a viable
tactic for "play to win" when you have a "no time limit" stipulation.

Think about your normal "casual" games. With competent players, how
long do they usually last? 1-3 hours seems to be enough to cover 99%
of the games, it's very rare to have any sort of extreme marathons.

I'm not saying it's a perfect solution. I'm just saying that it has
worked for me/us, and it can help to reduce the amount of intentional
stalling in games. That's all. If you don't see intentional stalling
as a problem, then go with the 2 hour limit. I myself do see it as a
problem, so I've tried to do something about it, with pretty good
success so far.

//Petri

And I pretty much agree with this as a practical solution.
Realistically, nobody is going to change the finals' rules so
dramatically that we don't have a declared winner (although
personally, I favor this "boot up the butt" approach).

And as LSJ pointed out, doing so is already completely within the
rules. Bonus.

And (the theory goes), you either tack on the amount of time people
essentially waste, making it pretty much identical with the earlier
game environment, or better yet, you set up a positive feedback loop
where people realize that the game is less likely to time out so they
don't bother trying to make it time out.

Which leaves the counterarguments to deal with. The first one I can
recall is "but that wouldn't be fair, because I built my deck to win
within 2 hours, not 2.5, and that's what got me into the finals."

Basically, I just don't buy it. I suppose it's *possible* for some
ubergenius to achieve that exact precision. But with the staggering
number of variables -- values for which nobody can have any
foreknowledge -- and always being subject to the mercies of random
distribution, I think it's a non sequitur no matter how smart you
think you are.

>From my point of view, it's possible to make meaningful alterations in
a deck based on whether it's going to be a four of five player game.
Put simply, you'll want more cards in a larger game, or might be
tempted to use variance in your favor with a smaller deck if you knew
you could do without the extra inventory.

People already chuck their decks into a 4/5 player churn (OK, maybe
not Paris or Budapest) without feeling crippled by it. So taking a
chance on *maybe* having to absorb the impact, on your deck
construction, of an extra 30 minutes on the clock, which is probably
just time lost thinking and talking, not the number of turns taken,
seems like a pretty small thing.

And anyway, if you can optimize your decks to do well in 2 hours at
the expense of doing poorly in 2.5, then I'm sure you can come up with
something equally fiendishly clever, knowing about the bizarro,
weirdly distorted final round ahead of time.

I suppose there are other counterarguments to deal with, but I think
that's the main one to overcome.

As a tournament judge with lots of tournaments under my belt... that'd
be a firm, resounding "no". Maybe I'm just a crap judge, but still:
"no".

Why? Because what happens is that certain players interrupt most
actions in the game with "hey, let's make a deal, I might have a DI"
gobbledegook. It's the way they play. When they want to stall, they
just do it more, and try to stretch out the "dealmaking". How are you,
as a judge, supposed to say "play A is valid tactical play" but "play
B is stalling"? The stalling player will just say that since it's a
final round, he has to do everything he can to get deals that are
favorable for him, and claim it's playing to win. It's one huge grey
area. Maybe you'd be fine with drawing some arbitrary line there, but
I'm not.

Removing time limits / stretching them out seems to work very well, so
I don't need to draw that line. If someone were to try to timeout a
game round that can potentially stretch out for 3-4 hours, they'd have
to be so completely blatant about it that a warning would be easy to
give.

With the current 2-hour limit, it's just too easy to just gabble a bit
more in the guise of "tactics", and stall the game out, while still
avoiding judge warnings (because they are so very very hard to call in
these cases). See the latest EC final rounds for one example.

Two reasons spring to mind.
1) you cite experience as a main motivator for how a judge uses his
judgement. If so, different experiences can easily (inevitably?) lead to
different judgements. The judge who has less experience with table talk
might not catch on to the incremental time use mentioned above until much
later than another judge. The resulting variation in the timing of a
penalty can have a big impact on the game; does the infraction get
penalized on the sixth instance of time use? The twelfth? If its left
to the judge's opinion, you must agree that each judge will likely havea
different answer to the same situation. Hence, inconsistent.
Same holds true for deal-making, decklist checks, etc. It really boils
down to "experience" is the same as "using one's judgement" is the same
as "opinion", and as we all know, opinions are as varied as snowflakes.
Indeed, your goading of Petri further down-thread is just an indication
that he has a different opinion of when its appropriate to judge, and
when it is not. In that sense, by saying there are no grounds for making
a judgement, and you are disagreeing with his particular "use of
judgement". You're being inconsistent, Damnans. :-)

2) Lack of training and examples of implementation. Even with 1, above,
we might overcome the issue by having _something_ in the way of training
and real examples recorded somewhere for judges to refer to, and get a
better insight into when and how the rules should be implemented on
nebulous topics such as time use and deal making. We don't, and what's
more, when a judge does rule on these topics, its pretty hotly debate,
_exactly because_ there are currently no grounds _other_ than opinion
upon which to base a ruling...

To be clear: Damnans, I hear what you're saying and actually agree
with parts of it. What I'm saying is that running the final round as
(effectively) unlimited by time has worked very well *for us*, during
that 10+ years I've been running big and small tournaments. Sure,
sometimes I need to set a limit because of real-life timetable issues,
but gamewise the no-limit style has worked very well with no real
drawbacks. It's popular with the players, and I like it too.

Now, partly that may be due to the Finnish metagame, which anyway
emphasises "play.the.game!" mentality and doesn't do the endless
tabletalk thing that central European gamers tend to go for. It might
well be that it would fail miserably in other contexts. I don't know.

It works for us, it might work for others. Will it solve all the
problems? Of course not.

Will it hurt players who optimize their decks to win in precisely 2
hours? Sure, a bit. Will it hurt players who just copy an old
tournament deck from the TWD archive and play that? Possibly. Thing
is, I don't see either of those as good things, so hurting them is
actually a bonus as far as I'm concerned :)

send all his imbued to the hospital :-); and I also knew that my
grandprey (who was playing Toreador vote) would not be able to oust the
imbued. So I chose to oust my prey when no one else could have enough
time to react and take the tournament win from me.
